simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #1: Ethereum went live on July 30, 2015, as a blockchain that runs programs, not just payments. This series opens the hood: accounts, gas, the EVM, staking, blobs. One mechanism a day. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #1: Ethereum mainnet (Frontier) launched July 30, 2015. Since then: about 20 network upgrades, a switch from proof-of-work to proof-of-stake and a data layer for rollups. This series covers how each piece works, one fact per post. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #2: Bitcoin tracks coins (unspent outputs). Ethereum tracks accounts, like a bank ledger: each address has a balance that goes up and down. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #2: Ethereum uses an account model, not UTXOs. Each account holds 4 fields: nonce, balance (in wei), storageRoot (root of its storage trie) and codeHash (hash of its code; for wallets, the hash of empty code). #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #3: Two kinds of accounts: ones controlled by a private key (your wallet) and ones controlled by code (smart contracts). Only key holders can start a transaction; contracts only react. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #3: Two account types: externally owned accounts (EOAs), controlled by a secp256k1 key, and contract accounts, controlled by EVM code. Only EOAs originate transactions; contracts run when called. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #4: Your Ethereum address is derived from your public key: hash it, keep the last 20 bytes. That's the 40 hex characters after 0x. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #4: An Ethereum address = last 20 bytes of Keccak-256(public key), where the key is the 64-byte uncompressed secp256k1 point (no 0x04 prefix). 20 bytes = 40 hex chars. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #5: Ever noticed addresses mix UPPER and lower case letters? It's not random: the pattern is a checksum that lets wallets catch typos. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #5: EIP-55 checksum: hash the lowercase hex address with Keccak-256; each letter is uppercased if the matching hash nibble is >= 8. A typo breaks the pattern with high probability. All-lowercase stays valid, just unchecked. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #6: Ethereum's hash function is often called SHA-3, but it isn't the official SHA-3. It uses the original Keccak, so the same input gives a different hash. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #6: Ethereum uses Keccak-256, not NIST SHA3-256. The permutation is the same, but FIPS 202 changed the padding (domain byte 0x06 vs Keccak's 0x01), so outputs differ. Solidity's keccak256() is the original Keccak. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #7: 1 ETH = 1,000,000,000,000,000,000 wei, the smallest unit. Gas prices use gwei: one billionth of an ETH. Under the hood, every balance is counted in wei. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #7: ETH denominations: 1 ETH = 10^18 wei; 1 gwei = 10^9 wei. Older named units: szabo (10^12 wei) and finney (10^15 wei). The protocol only knows wei: balances and a tx's value field are in wei. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #8: An Ethereum transaction has no 'from' field. Nodes work out who sent it from the signature itself. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #8: There is no sender field in an Ethereum transaction. Nodes recover the signer's public key from the ECDSA signature (v, r, s) and derive the address. The same idea powers the ecrecover precompile at address 0x01. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #9: Every wallet has a counter called a nonce. Each transaction uses the next number, so the same transaction can't be replayed and order is guaranteed. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #9: An EOA's nonce = number of transactions it has sent. A tx must carry exactly the current nonce, so txs from one account run in strict order and can't be replayed. Reusing a nonce with a higher fee is how wallets 'speed up' or cancel. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #10: Why can't a transaction signed for Ethereum be replayed on another chain? Since 2016, each signature includes the chain's ID. Ethereum mainnet is chain 1. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #10: EIP-155 (Spurious Dragon, Nov 2016) mixes the chain ID into the signed data: v = chainId*2 + 35 or 36. A tx signed for mainnet (chain ID 1) is invalid on Ethereum Classic or a testnet. Typed txs carry chainId as a field. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #11: An ECDSA signature has a 'mirror twin' that is also valid. Since 2016, Ethereum only accepts one of the two, so nobody can tweak a signature to change a tx's ID. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #11: EIP-2 (Homestead, 2016) rejects tx signatures with s > secp256k1n/2. For every valid (r, s) there is a twin (r, n-s); allowing only the low one removes signature malleability and changes to the tx hash. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #12: Every action on Ethereum costs 'gas', a unit of work. A plain ETH transfer always costs 21,000 gas. Running a contract costs more, depending on what it does. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #12: Every EVM opcode has a gas cost; a tx pays gas_used * gas price. A plain ETH transfer costs the intrinsic 21,000 gas. The gas limit field caps what a tx may use; if it runs out, its changes are reverted but the gas is still paid. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #13: How big can a block be? Validators decide together: each new block can move the limit only a tiny step up or down. For Fusaka (Dec 2025), clients' default target was raised to 60 million gas. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #13: The block gas limit is voted by proposers: each block may change it by < 1/1024 of the parent's limit. EIP-7935 had clients raise their default target from 36M (Apr 2025) to 60M gas ahead of Fusaka. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #14: Ethereum's first blocks were almost empty on purpose: at launch each block was capped at 5,000 gas, not even enough for one transfer. The cap was lifted at block 200,000. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #14: Frontier genesis set a 5,000 gas limit per block, below the 21,000 gas of a transfer, so early blocks held no txs. 'Frontier Thawing' at block 200,000 (Sep 7, 2015) lifted it and set a new default gas price. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #15: Since August 2021, part of every Ethereum fee is destroyed (burned). This 'base fee' rises when blocks are full and falls when they are empty. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #15: EIP-1559 (London, Aug 5, 2021): each block has a base fee that is burned. It moves by up to 12.5% per block, up if the parent used more gas than the target, down if less. #ETH #SmartContracts
variant: #Ethereum Deep Dive #15: Part of every fee paid on Ethereum since 2021 has simply vanished, on purpose. EIP-1559 burns the 'base fee' of every transaction instead of paying it to the block producer. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #16: With EIP-1559 you set a maximum price and a tip. You pay the network's current base fee plus your tip, never more than your max. The rest stays in your wallet. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #16: Type-2 txs set maxFeePerGas and maxPriorityFeePerGas. Effective price = base fee + min(tip, maxFee - base fee). The base fee part is burned, the tip goes to the proposer, and the unused margin is never charged. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #17: Ethereum blocks aim to be half full. Busy periods can fill them up to double that target, and the fee goes up until demand calms down. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #17: EIP-1559 elasticity multiplier = 2: gas target = gas limit / 2. A block can use up to 2x target; the base fee update is proportional to (gas_used - target) / target / 8, hence the 12.5% max step. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #18: Ethereum supports several transaction formats. Since 2021, the first byte of a transaction says which type it is, so new kinds can be added without breaking old ones. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #18: EIP-2718 (Berlin, Apr 2021) added typed tx envelopes: TransactionType || payload. Types today: 0 legacy, 1 access list (EIP-2930), 2 fee market (EIP-1559), 3 blob (EIP-4844), 4 set-code (EIP-7702). #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #19: A transaction can come with a list of the addresses and storage it will touch. Declaring them up front makes that access a bit cheaper. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #19: EIP-2930 (Berlin) type-1 txs carry an access list of addresses and storage keys. Listed items are pre-warmed: 2,400 gas per address and 1,900 per key up front, then warm-access pricing during execution. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #20: Reading contract data costs much more the first time in a transaction than the second time. The first read is 'cold', later reads are 'warm'. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #20: EIP-2929 (Berlin): first access to a storage slot costs 2,100 gas (cold SLOAD), first touch of an account 2,600; later accesses in the same tx are warm at 100 gas. It was a response to DoS attacks using cheap state reads. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #21: Sending data inside a transaction costs gas per byte. Zero bytes are cheaper than non-zero bytes, which is why addresses with many leading zeros save a little. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #21: Calldata pricing: 4 gas per zero byte, 16 per non-zero byte. EIP-2028 (Istanbul, Dec 2019) cut the non-zero price from 68 to 16 gas, which made rollups posting data to L1 much cheaper. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #22: Since Pectra (May 2025), transactions that mostly carry data and do little computing pay a higher minimum price. The goal: push bulk data toward blobs. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #22: EIP-7623 (Pectra) adds a calldata floor price: if a tx spends little gas on execution, it pays at least 10 gas per zero byte and 40 per non-zero byte. This caps worst-case block size. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #23: Since Fusaka (Dec 2025), one transaction can't use more than about 16.8 million gas, however big blocks get. No single transaction can hog a whole block. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #23: EIP-7825 (Fusaka) caps gas per tx at 16,777,216 (2^24). Blocks can keep growing, but heavy work must be split across txs, which helps future parallel execution and bounds worst-case validation time. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #24: The Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) is a simple computer every node runs in exactly the same way. Same input, same result, on every machine on Earth. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #24: The EVM is a stack machine with 256-bit words and a max stack depth of 1024. Execution is deterministic: every node replays every tx and must reach the same state root, or it rejects the block. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #25: Each contract has its own giant key-value store with 2^256 slots. Writing a new value there is one of the most expensive things you can do on Ethereum. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #25: Contract storage maps 2^256 keys to 32-byte values. SSTORE from zero to non-zero costs 20,000 gas (plus 2,100 if the slot is cold), while a warm SLOAD is 100. Saving storage writes is the core of gas optimization. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #26: Contracts also get scratch memory that is wiped after each call. It's cheap at first, but the price climbs faster and faster as you use more of it. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #26: EVM memory is a byte array that lives only for the call. Expansion cost = 3*words + words^2/512 (words of 32 bytes), so it is quadratic: cheap for KBs, prohibitive for many MBs. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #27: Since March 2024, contracts have a third kind of memory: data that lasts for a whole transaction, then disappears. Handy for locks against reentrancy attacks. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #27: EIP-1153 (Dencun) adds TSTORE/TLOAD: transient storage that persists across calls within one tx and is cleared at the end. Each costs 100 gas, far below SSTORE; typical uses: reentrancy locks, single-tx token approvals. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #28: Freeing storage used to earn back a big gas refund, so people 'banked' gas in tokens when it was cheap. A 2021 change cut refunds and killed that trick. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #28: EIP-3529 (London) removed the SELFDESTRUCT refund, lowered the SSTORE clear refund and capped refunds at gas_used/5 (was /2). GasToken-style tricks became worthless. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #29: When a contract calls another, it can't hand over all its remaining gas: it always keeps a small part back. This rule stopped a whole family of attacks. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #29: EIP-150 (Tangerine Whistle, Oct 2016): a CALL can forward at most 63/64 of remaining gas. Each nested call keeps 1/64 back, which makes the 1024 call-depth attack impractical and lets callers handle failures. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #30: If a contract hits a problem, it can cancel everything it did and give back the gas it didn't use, along with a reason. Before 2017 a failure burned all the gas. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #30: REVERT (EIP-140, Byzantium, Oct 2017) aborts execution, rolls back state changes, refunds remaining gas and returns data (e.g. a revert reason). Before, aborting meant running out of gas or an invalid opcode, both burning all gas. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #31: Contracts can call others in 'read-only' mode. If the called code tries to change anything, the call fails. Useful for price checks and views. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #31: STATICCALL (EIP-214, Byzantium) runs a call where any state change (SSTORE, LOG, CREATE, value transfer, SELFDESTRUCT) makes it fail. Solidity uses it for view and pure function calls. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #32: A contract can borrow another contract's code and run it on its own data. That's how 'upgradeable' contracts work: the code can be swapped, the data stays. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #32: DELEGATECALL (EIP-7, Homestead) executes the target's code in the caller's context: same storage, msg.sender and msg.value. It's the basis of libraries and proxy patterns like EIP-1967 upgradeable proxies. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #33: In Nov 2017, a user killed a shared library contract that hundreds of Parity wallets relied on. About 514,000 ETH has been stuck in those wallets ever since. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #33: Parity multisig, Nov 6, 2017: the library behind the wallets was uninitialized. Someone called initWallet to become owner, then kill() (SELFDESTRUCT). The 587 wallets that DELEGATECALLed into it froze ≈513,774 ETH. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #34: Smart contracts have a size limit: about 24 KB of code. Big apps have to split their logic across several contracts. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #34: EIP-170 (Spurious Dragon, Nov 2016) caps deployed contract code at 24,576 bytes (0x6000). It bounds the DoS cost of loading code; it's why large protocols use libraries, proxies or the diamond pattern. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #35: The code that sets up a new contract also has a size limit, double the contract limit, and it's charged per chunk. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #35: EIP-3860 (Shanghai, Apr 2023) limits initcode to 49,152 bytes (2x the EIP-170 limit) and charges 2 gas per 32-byte word of initcode, since nodes had to analyze it for jump destinations without charge. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #36: Since 2021, no new contract can start with the byte 0xEF. That byte is reserved so future versions of contract code can be told apart. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #36: EIP-3541 (London) rejects new contract code starting with 0xEF. It reserved the prefix for EOF (EVM Object Format) and later used it for EIP-7702 delegation designators, which begin with 0xef0100. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #37: You can know a contract's address before it exists: it's computed from the creator's address and how many contracts it has deployed so far. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #37: CREATE address = last 20 bytes of Keccak-256(RLP([sender, nonce])). For an EOA, the nonce is its tx count; for a contract, its creation count. So addresses are predictable but tied to deployment order. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #38: Since 2019, a contract can be deployed to an address chosen in advance, whatever happens in between. Used for counterfactual wallets and same addresses on many chains. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #38: CREATE2 (EIP-1014, Constantinople, Feb 2019): address = last 20 bytes of Keccak-256(0xff ++ sender ++ salt ++ Keccak-256(init_code)). It depends on salt and code, not nonce, so it can be used before deployment. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #39: Contracts used to be able to delete themselves. Since March 2024, that only works in the same transaction that created them. Otherwise, the ETH is sent away but the code stays. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #39: EIP-6780 (Dencun): SELFDESTRUCT only deletes code and storage if called in the tx that created the contract. Otherwise it just sends the balance to the target. This ended the CREATE2 'metamorphic contract' trick. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #40: How does a contract know which function you're calling? The first 4 bytes of your transaction data name it, derived from a hash of the function's name. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #40: Function selector = first 4 bytes of Keccak-256 of the signature, e.g. transfer(address,uint256) = 0xa9059cbb. Arguments follow, ABI-encoded in 32-byte words. With only 32 bits, selector clashes are possible. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #41: When a contract does something worth noticing (a transfer, a swap), it can emit an 'event'. Wallets and explorers read these events to show your history. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #41: LOG0-LOG4 write events to the tx receipt with up to 4 indexed 32-byte topics; topic 0 is usually the event signature hash. Each block header has a 2048-bit logs bloom for quick filtering. Contracts can't read logs. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #42: Some built-in contracts live at tiny addresses like 0x01. They do heavy cryptography natively, much cheaper than writing it in contract code. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #42: Precompiles: 0x01 ecrecover, 0x02 SHA-256, 0x03 RIPEMD-160, 0x04 identity, 0x05 modexp, 0x06-0x08 BN254 ops, 0x09 BLAKE2f, 0x0a KZG point evaluation, 0x0b-0x11 BLS12-381. 0x100 is secp256r1 (P-256). #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #43: Zero-knowledge proofs on Ethereum became practical in 2017, when built-in operations for a special elliptic curve were added. Many zk apps still rely on them. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #43: Byzantium (Oct 2017) added BN254 (alt_bn128) precompiles: point addition, scalar multiplication (EIP-196) and pairing check (EIP-197) at 0x06-0x08, enough to verify Groth16 zk-SNARKs on-chain. Istanbul cut their gas (EIP-1108). #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #44: Since May 2025, contracts can natively check BLS signatures, the same kind Ethereum validators use. That makes it cheaper to verify the consensus layer from inside a contract. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #44: EIP-2537 (Pectra) adds BLS12-381 precompiles at 0x0b-0x11: G1/G2 addition and multi-scalar multiplication, pairing check and map-to-curve. Per the EIP: 120+ bits of security, vs 80 bits for the older BN254 precompile. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #45: Since Fusaka (Dec 2025), Ethereum can check signatures from phone secure chips and passkeys natively. A step toward wallets you unlock with Face ID. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #45: EIP-7951 (Fusaka) adds a secp256r1 (P-256) verification precompile. P-256 is the curve of FIDO2/WebAuthn passkeys, Apple Secure Enclave and Android Keystore, so smart wallets can verify them cheaply. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #46: Sometimes small things matter: in 2023 the EVM got an instruction that just pushes the number zero. It saves a little gas in almost every contract. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #46: PUSH0 (EIP-3855, Shanghai) pushes 0 on the stack for 2 gas and 1 byte. Before, compilers used PUSH1 0x00 (3 gas, 2 bytes) or tricks like RETURNDATASIZE. Solidity has targeted it by default since 0.8.20. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #47: Fusaka (Dec 2025) added a new EVM instruction that counts leading zero bits in a number. Useful for math libraries and compression. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #47: EIP-7939 (Fusaka) adds CLZ: count leading zeros of a 256-bit word (returns 256 for 0). It replaces costly bit-by-bit loops in log2, sqrt and fixed-point math. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #48: A contract can only look up the hash of the last 256 blocks. Since Pectra (May 2025), the chain also keeps the last 8,191 block hashes in a system contract. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #48: BLOCKHASH only covers the 256 most recent blocks (0 otherwise). EIP-2935 (Pectra) stores the last 8,191 block hashes in a system contract's storage, so contracts and stateless clients can prove against older blocks. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #49: Contracts can get a random-looking number from the consensus layer since the Merge. It's useful but not perfect: a block proposer can bias it slightly. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #49: EIP-4399 (Paris) repurposed the DIFFICULTY opcode (0x44) as PREVRANDAO: the beacon chain's RANDAO mix. A proposer can only publish or skip its block, so it gets about 1 bit of influence. Not safe for high-value lotteries. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #50: Since March 2024, contracts can read a fingerprint of the consensus layer's latest blocks. That lets staking apps check validator data without trusting an oracle. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #50: EIP-4788 (Dencun) stores each parent beacon block root in a system contract (ring buffer of 8,191 entries). Contracts can verify Merkle proofs of beacon state: balances, withdrawals, validator status. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #51: The whole state of Ethereum (every balance and contract) is summarized by one 32-byte fingerprint in each block header. Change one balance and it changes completely. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #51: Ethereum stores state in a Merkle Patricia Trie keyed by Keccak-256(address). Each header commits to stateRoot, transactionsRoot and receiptsRoot, so any account can be proven against a header with a Merkle proof. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #52: Ethereum has its own simple way to turn data into bytes, called RLP. It only knows two things: strings of bytes and lists. Everything else is built from those. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #52: RLP (Recursive Length Prefix) encodes byte strings and nested lists only. Prefix ranges: 0x00-0x7f single byte, 0x80-0xbf strings, 0xc0-0xff lists. The consensus layer uses a different format, SSZ. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #53: In June 2016, a hacker drained ETH from The DAO, a huge investment contract. Ethereum chose to rewrite history to return the funds. Those who refused kept the old chain: Ethereum Classic. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #53: The DAO was drained via reentrancy in June 2016 (about 3.6M ETH). The DAO fork at block 1,920,000 (Jul 20, 2016) moved its funds to a withdrawal contract. Miners and users who rejected it kept running Ethereum Classic. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #54: Ethereum had a built-in 'bomb' that made mining harder and harder over time, to force the move to proof-of-stake. It was pushed back several times before the Merge. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #54: The difficulty bomb (Ice Age) added an exponential term to PoW difficulty. It was delayed by EIP-649 (Byzantium), EIP-1234, EIP-2384 (Muir Glacier), EIP-3554, EIP-4345 (Arrow Glacier) and EIP-5133 (Gray Glacier). #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #55: Before 2022, Ethereum was mined. Its mining algorithm needed lots of memory on purpose, so ordinary graphics cards could compete with specialized machines. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #55: Ethereum PoW used Ethash: each hash reads pseudo-random pages from a multi-GB dataset (the DAG) that grew every epoch of 30,000 blocks. Memory bandwidth, not raw compute, was the bottleneck, which favored GPUs. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #56: Miners' reward per block fell over time: 5 ETH at launch, then 3 ETH in 2017, then 2 ETH in 2019. After the Merge, mining rewards stopped completely. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #56: PoW block reward: 5 ETH from genesis, 3 ETH at Byzantium (EIP-649, Oct 2017), 2 ETH at Constantinople (EIP-1234, Feb 2019). At the Merge (Sep 2022) rewards moved to validators on the beacon chain. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #57: In the mining days, a valid block that lost the race still earned a reward if a later block mentioned it. These were called uncle blocks. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #57: PoW Ethereum rewarded ommers (uncles): valid stale blocks included by a later block within 6 generations. This lowered the edge of large, well-connected pools. Proof-of-stake removed them; ommersHash is now a constant. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #58: Ethereum's proof-of-stake chain started on Dec 1, 2020, running alongside the mined chain for almost 2 years. It needed 16,384 validators of 32 ETH each to start. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #58: Beacon Chain genesis: Dec 1, 2020, after the deposit contract reached the minimum of 16,384 validators of 32 ETH. It ran in parallel with PoW mainnet, only coming to consensus on itself, until the Merge. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #59: Every Ethereum validator starts with a deposit to one contract, deployed on Oct 14, 2020. Its address starts with eight zeros: 0x00000000219ab5... #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #59: The staking deposit contract 0x00000000219ab540356cBB839Cbe05303d7705Fa was deployed Oct 14, 2020 at block 11,052,984. It keeps an incremental Merkle tree of deposits that the consensus layer reads. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #60: The Merge wasn't set for a block number or a date. It was triggered when the total mining work ever done on Ethereum crossed a fixed threshold. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #60: The Merge was triggered by a Terminal Total Difficulty of 58,750,000,000,000,000,000,000. The first PoW block whose cumulative difficulty passed it became the last PoW block; a block-height trigger could have been gamed. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #61: On Sep 15, 2022, Ethereum switched from miners to stakers without stopping. Block 15,537,394 was the first one produced by proof-of-stake. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #61: Paris (the Merge), Sep 15, 2022: block 15,537,394 was the first PoS execution block. EIP-3675 removed PoW validity rules, and the Engine API made the beacon chain drive the execution layer. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #62: The Merge cut Ethereum's energy use by more than 99.98%. Validating with staked ETH needs ordinary computers, not warehouses of mining rigs. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #62: Per ethereum.org (CCRI estimate), moving from PoW to PoS cut Ethereum's electricity use by more than 99.98%. Security now comes from ETH at stake that can be slashed, not from electricity spent on hashing. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #63: An Ethereum node is two programs working together: one runs transactions and contracts, the other agrees with other nodes on which block comes next. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #63: Since the Merge, a node pairs an execution client (Geth, Nethermind, Besu, Erigon, Reth...) with a consensus client (Prysm, Lighthouse, Teku, Nimbus, Lodestar, Grandine). They talk via the authenticated Engine API. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #64: Ethereum time runs in 12-second 'slots', each with a chance for one block. 32 slots make an 'epoch' of 6.4 minutes. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #64: Beacon chain timing: SECONDS_PER_SLOT = 12, SLOTS_PER_EPOCH = 32, so an epoch is 384 s = 6.4 min. A slot can be empty if its proposer is offline; the chain doesn't wait. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #65: On Ethereum, a block becomes 'final' (cannot be reversed without destroying a huge amount of staked ETH) after about 13 minutes. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #65: Casper FFG finality: an epoch checkpoint is justified when attestations from 2/3 of total stake vote for it, and finalized when the next checkpoint is justified on top. Typically about 2 epochs (12.8 min). #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #66: If two versions of the chain compete, nodes follow the one most validators recently voted for. This rule picks the head of the chain every slot. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #66: Fork choice is LMD-GHOST: starting from the last justified checkpoint, at each fork follow the branch with the most weight from each validator's latest attestation. Gasper combines it with Casper FFG. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #67: Every active validator votes once per epoch (every 6.4 minutes). Validators are randomly split into small groups so no single block gets all the votes at once. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #67: Each epoch, validators are shuffled into committees across the 32 slots (target committee size 128, up to 64 committees per slot). Each attestation votes for a head block and the source and target checkpoints. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #68: Who proposes the next block? A random draw weighted by stake. Since Fusaka (Dec 2025), the proposer schedule is fixed in advance and visible on-chain. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #68: Proposers are picked from RANDAO randomness, weighted by effective balance. EIP-7917 (Fusaka) makes the proposer lookahead deterministic and stores it in beacon state, which helps preconfirmation designs. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #69: Hundreds of thousands of validators vote every few minutes. Ethereum can handle it because their signatures can be squeezed together into one. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #69: The consensus layer signs with BLS12-381. Signatures on the same message aggregate into one 96-byte signature that verifies against the aggregate key, so a committee's votes cost about one check. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #70: Light wallets can follow Ethereum without downloading it, thanks to a small rotating group of 512 validators that sign every block header. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #70: Altair (Oct 2021) added sync committees: 512 validators picked every 256 epochs (about 27 h) sign each head. Light clients verify one aggregate BLS signature instead of following the full beacon chain. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #71: Validators who cheat get 'slashed': part of their stake is destroyed and they are kicked out. Cheating means signing two conflicting blocks or votes. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #71: Slashable offenses: proposing two different blocks for the same slot, double voting (two attestations, same target epoch) and surround voting (one vote's source-target span contains another's). #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #72: A lone validator slashed by mistake loses a small amount. But if many get slashed at the same time, each loses much more, possibly all its stake. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #72: Slashing: an initial cut (1/4096 of effective balance since Pectra's EIP-7251, was 1/32), then a correlation penalty about 18 days later, scaled by the total stake slashed around that time. Mass slashings can take everything. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #73: If over a third of validators go offline, the chain stops finalizing. The offline ones then slowly lose stake until the active ones are back above two-thirds. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #73: Inactivity leak: after 4 epochs without finality, inactive validators' balances drain faster and faster. Their share of stake shrinks until active validators hold 2/3 again and finality resumes. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #74: The more ETH is staked, the less each validator earns in percentage terms. Total new ETH issued grows much slower than the amount staked. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #74: Rewards are built from a base reward proportional to effective_balance / sqrt(total active stake). Issuance grows with the square root of stake, so per-validator yield falls as more ETH is staked. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #75: Staked ETH could not be withdrawn at all until April 12, 2023. Since then, rewards above the stake are paid out to validators' wallets automatically. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #75: Shapella (Apr 12, 2023) enabled withdrawals (EIP-4895). A sweep scans validators in order and puts up to 16 withdrawals in each block: partial (excess balance) or full (exited). No tx or gas needed. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #76: A validator used to be capped at 32 ETH. Since May 2025, one validator can hold up to 2,048 ETH, so big stakers need far fewer of them. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #76: EIP-7251 (Pectra, May 7, 2025) raises MAX_EFFECTIVE_BALANCE to 2048 ETH for validators with 0x02 credentials; minimum stays 32. Rewards above 32 can auto-compound and validators can be consolidated. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #77: Since May 2025, the wallet that receives a validator's withdrawals can also force it to exit. Before, only the validator's signing key could. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #77: EIP-7002 (Pectra) lets the withdrawal credential address trigger exits and partial withdrawals from the execution layer via a system contract, without the validator key. Useful for staking pools and contracts. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #78: Starting to stake used to mean waiting about 12 hours just for your deposit to be seen. Since May 2025, it takes about 13 minutes. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #78: EIP-6110 (Pectra) moves deposits in-protocol: the execution layer passes them to the consensus layer directly, instead of the old eth1 data voting. The delay drops from about 12 h to about 13 min. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #79: Validators can't all join or leave at once: there's a queue with a cap per epoch. It keeps the validator set stable and finality safe. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #79: Churn limits throttle entries and exits. EIP-7514 (Dencun) capped activations at 8 validators per epoch. Pectra (EIP-7251) switched to an ETH-based churn, capped at 256 ETH per epoch. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #80: Ethereum runs on many independent software versions written by different teams. If one has a bug, the others keep the chain going. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #80: Client diversity matters: a bug in a consensus client run by > 1/3 of nodes could stop finality; with > 2/3, it could finalize an invalid chain. Ideally no client exceeds 33%. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #81: Many validators don't build their own blocks. They let specialized 'builders' assemble them and pick the one that pays best. This happens outside the core protocol. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #81: MEV-Boost (Flashbots) is out-of-protocol proposer-builder separation: builders send blocks to relays, relays pick the most profitable one for the proposer, whose consensus client then publishes it. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #82: Since March 2024, Ethereum has 'blobs': big chunks of cheap data, about 128 KB each, used by rollups to post their transactions. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #82: EIP-4844 (Dencun, Mar 13, 2024): type-3 txs carry blobs of 4,096 field elements x 32 bytes = 131,072 bytes (128 KiB). The EVM can't read blob content, only a versioned hash of its KZG commitment. #ETH #SmartContracts
variant: #Ethereum Deep Dive #82: Layer 2 fees dropped sharply in March 2024. Why? Ethereum added 'blobs', a cheap data lane built for rollups, each about 128 KB. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #83: Blobs don't stay on Ethereum forever: nodes delete them after about 18 days. That's long enough for anyone to check the data, and keeps nodes light. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #83: Consensus nodes must serve blob data for 4096 epochs (about 18 days), then may prune it: MIN_EPOCHS_FOR_BLOB_SIDECARS_REQUESTS, and its data column twin since Fusaka's PeerDAS. Only the commitment stays in blocks permanently. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #84: Blobs have their own fee, separate from normal gas. When few rollups need space, blob fees can be close to zero even if regular gas is expensive. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #84: EIP-4844 adds a separate blob gas market with its own 1559-style base fee, also burned. Each blob uses 2^17 = 131,072 blob gas. At Dencun the target was 3 blobs per block, the max 6. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #85: Blobs rely on special cryptography that needed a one-time setup. Over 141,000 contributions were made in 2023; it's secure if just one contributor was honest. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #85: Blob KZG commitments need a trusted setup. The KZG ceremony ran 208 days (Jan 13 - Aug 8, 2023) and got 141,416 contributions. Its security assumption: at least one participant kept its secret hidden. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #86: Pectra (May 2025) doubled the blob target, from 3 to 6 per block, with a max of 9. More room for rollups. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #86: EIP-7691 (Pectra, May 2025) raised the blob target/max from 3/6 to 6/9 per block, the baseline that Fusaka then built on with Blob Parameter Only forks. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #87: Since Fusaka (Dec 2025), nodes don't download every blob. They check random pieces, like spot-checking a book, and are confident the whole data was published. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #87: PeerDAS (EIP-7594, Fusaka, Dec 3, 2025): blob data is erasure-coded and split so each node only downloads and checks samples. Sampling gives high confidence the full data was published, without every node fetching it all. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #88: Ethereum can now raise blob capacity with mini-upgrades that change only that setting. Two followed Fusaka: Dec 2025 and Jan 2026. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #88: EIP-7892 'Blob Parameter Only' forks change only blob target/max. BPO1 (Dec 9, 2025) set 10/15, BPO2 (Jan 7, 2026) set 14/21, up from 6/9 at Fusaka activation. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #89: Blob fees used to fall to almost nothing, even when the network was busy. Since Fusaka (Dec 2025), blobs pay a minimum linked to the price of regular gas. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #89: EIP-7918 (Fusaka) bounds the blob base fee by execution cost: when the blob base fee is too low relative to the execution base fee, it stops falling. That ends 1-wei blob fees during busy periods. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #90: Since May 2025, a regular wallet can act like a smart contract wallet: batch transactions, have someone else pay gas, add spending rules, without changing its address. #ETH #SmartContracts
tech: #Ethereum Deep Dive #90: EIP-7702 (Pectra) type-4 tx: an EOA signs an authorization that sets its code to 0xef0100 || address, a pointer to a contract. Calls then run that code in the EOA's context, so pick the delegate with care. #ETH #SmartContracts

simple: #Ethereum Deep Dive #91: Ethereum in one breath: accounts, gas, a shared virtual machine, proof-of-stake with 12 s slots, blobs for rollups. Follow @xcryptokeys for one deep dive a day. #ETH #SmartContracts
